sentences.text: Most species of this dinosaur measured roughly 15 to 26 meters in length, though some estimates based on undescribed vertebrae suggest they could reach up to 35 meters.
The holotype of M. youngi is very complete, featuring an articulated vertebral column from the first cervical to the eighth tail vertebra and a nearly complete skull.
M. jingyanensis possessed a femur length of 2 meters.
Mamenchisaurus constructus, known from a single skeleton, is estimated to be 13 to 15 meters in length.
The genus Mamenchisaurus was established by Professor C. C. Young in 1954, with the type species named Mamenchisaurus constructus.
This species received its name because the first fossil was found during construction work.
The name Mamenchisaurus means 'Mamenchi lizard', derived from Chinese Pinyin for 'horse', 'gate', and 'stream' combined with the Greek suffix for 'lizard'.
Mamenchisaurus hochuanensis was described in 1972 by Young and Xijin Zhao.
Analysis suggests the neck of M. youngi was kept mostly straight, with possible flexibility at the base and near the head.
Bone histology analysis of a Mamenchisaurus ulna estimated the age at death to be 43 years.
Mamenchisaurus is classified within the family Mamenchisauridae.
Researchers sometimes refer to Mamenchisaurus as a 'wastebasket taxon' due to questions about the number of species and fragmentary specimens assigned to it.
Mamenchisaurus fossils range from the Late Jurassic to the Early Cretaceous, with a possible record during the Albian stage.
Fossils of Mamenchisaurus have been found in the Sichuan Basin and Yunnan Province in China.
M. sinocanadorum dates to the Oxfordian stage (161.2 to 158.7 mya) and M. anyuensis to the Aptian stage (around 114.4 mya).
M. anyuensis fossils are found in the top of the Suining Formation and the bottom of the Penglaizhen Formation.
Researchers could not support the referral of large vertebrae to M. sinocanadorum because they lack anatomical overlap with the type specimen.
The validity of numerous species assigned to the genus Mamenchisaurus has been questioned.
Researchers suggest M. anyuensis is unlikely to be a member of the genus Mamenchisaurus because it is roughly 30 million years younger than other species.
The validity of transferring species from other genera to Mamenchisaurus is disputed by researchers.
